title: Pulsatile signalling may let cells behaviour-shape each other in vivo

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Pulsatile signalling may let cells behaviour-shape each other in vivo

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because transcriptional and other signalling mechanisms are pulsatile, cells may apply timed behaviour-shaping stimuli to each other in vivo, exploiting the trainability of their pathways to evolve complex phenotypes, though the role of trainability in evolution and development is unknown.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Biswas S 2022, Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions › 3. Discussion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The role of trainability in evolution and development is as yet unknown, but it is interesting that transcriptional [126] and other [127,128] biological signaling mechanisms are now seen as pulsatile, which affords rich opportunity for cells to apply timed “behavior shaping” stimuli to each other in vivo, as a way of exploiting the multiscale competency of biological material to evolve complex phenotypes [129].

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Biswas S, Clawson W, Levin M, “Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions”, International journal of molecular sciences (2022), doi:10.3390/ijms24010285; section “3. Discussion”. Scope: Cells and tissues in vivo

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-grn-learning-22: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism has measurable consequences, but the necessary joint in vivo time series and interventions are not identified in current public resources. New perturbation experiments are likely required.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure natural intercellular pulse sequences, pathway-state changes, and resulting developmental phenotypes, then test whether disrupting pulse timing specifically removes history-dependent pathway shaping. Existing pulsatility alone does not demonstrate evolved behaviour-shaping.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public datasets rarely pair pulse-resolved signalling with pathway memory and morphology.

The evolutionary function is difficult to distinguish from ordinary signalling.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.18
analysis feasibility: 0.32
operationalizability: 0.58
data existence: 0.25

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The in vivo claim needs timed stimuli between cells and a persistent change in the receiver pathway. Existing pathway models show in silico trainability, and pulsatile transcription is reported in the literature, but no public dataset contains both sides of this interaction. A decisive test would be a new, or newly deposited, paired measurement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In living cells, record pulsatile signals from one cell and test whether a neighbour's pathway shows a persistent, specific change in a later response that meets the paper's memory criteria and that is absent without the pulses. That paired result would support in vivo behaviour-shaping; pulses without a lasting change in the neighbour would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The role in evolution and development is explicitly left unknown, so phenotype complexity alone does not decide it.

Public pulse-imaging studies do not pair an intercellular pulse train with a later memory assay on the target pathway.
